Confident, Fast, and Sometimes Wrong
What AI actually changes in a student's life, and what still gets in the way.
Project type: UX research
Method: 6 semi-structured interviews, analyzed via affinity diagramming
Audience: Postgraduate computer science students (master's and PhD, studying abroad)
Instructor: Arghavan Saeidan
It's 11pm. A grad student is staring at a bug that won't die. The honest choice is three days of documentation, or one prompt into a chat wi
They pick the chat window. This time, it works.
Next time, the same confident tone hands them a completely wrong answer, and they don't catch it until it's too late.
That gap — between getting help and getting fooled — is exactly where this research lives. Not whether grad students use AI. They all do. Bu

Six Things I Didn't Expect to Hear So Clearly
Six themes came out of the affinity mapping, clear enough that I didn't have to squint to see them. Here's what grad students actually told
1. Specific Tasks, Not General Chat
Every student I talked to used AI constantly, but not as a general chatbot. Their use cases were specific: paraphrasing dense text, debuggin
🗯️❝ I often rely on AI to summarize articles or provide insights into complex topics, which saves me a lot of time.❞
2. The time saved is not small. It's dramatic
This wasn't a marginal efficiency gain. Students described AI turning multi day problems into a matter of hours.
🗯️❝ Instead of spending several days reading through documentation, I can resolve problems in just a few hours with AI.❞
This is the strongest, clearest value in the whole study, and also the highest bar anything else has to clear. Anything that adds friction i
3. Two very different walls: money and permission
The barriers weren't really technical. They were structural. Cost was one. Premium tools are expensive enough that students described poolin
🗯️❝ It's quite expensive, but we're considering sharing an account to make it more manageable.❞
The other wall was institutional permission. Supervisors sometimes explicitly discouraged AI use, cutting students off from a tool they'd al
🗯️❝ My manager doesn't allow us to use AI tools for our projects, which makes it difficult for me to get help.❞
Together, these describe a group that wants in, but is being priced or policy blocked out.
4. Underneath the enthusiasm, a quiet worry about learning
Not everything was positive. A few students voiced something easy to miss if you only look at usage numbers: the worry that leaning on AI fo
🗯️❝ I feel like I'm relying on AI for quick fixes rather than truly understanding the material.❞
The fastest answer isn't always the one people actually want, especially when learning is the point.
Sounding Sure Isn't Being Right
Sounding Sure Isn't Being Right
Students had learned, the hard way, that AI's tone has nothing to do with its accuracy.
🗯️❝ Sometimes, AI gives me confident answers that turn out to be completely wrong.❞
They've already internalized the need to double check everything. But right now, they're doing all of that verification work alone, with no
6. Worried about the job market, but not panicking
Given how central AI already is to their work, I expected more anxiety about job security. What I found instead was a kind of measured confi
🗯️❝ While I think the way we approach our work may change, I'm sure there will always be a place for humans in the workforce.❞
They expect their methods to shift. They don't expect to be replaced, and they still trust their own judgment more than the tool's.
